name: Ariel Méndez
reasoning: A former Bend Bikes board president (2016-2019), Citywide Transportation Advisory Committee member, and current Transportation Bond Oversight Committee member, Méndez framed safer streets and reduced car-dependency as his central transportation vision upon taking office, explicitly tying it to walking/biking safety and fewer households needing two cars. This matches the most pedestrian/cycling/transit-forward end of the scale rather than a road-capacity focus.
quote_text: We will provide a safer community, a community where people don't have to worry about taking their lives in their hands when they're riding a bike or crossing the street. It will be lower costs. People won't spend as much time at the pump. Maybe some families will be able to get around with one car.

name: Ariel Méndez
reasoning: Méndez has been the council's point person explaining Bend's climate pollution fee (Bend Municipal Code Ch. 18.20, adopted by roll-call vote June 17, 2026), a social-cost-of-carbon-based fee on emissions sources whose revenue funds climate and infrastructure programs; as of December 2025 he described the fee as limited to new development only. This is a real carbon-pricing/investment mechanism rather than a fossil-fuel ban or aggressive 2030 phase-out mandate, matching the 'invest in clean energy while gradually reducing reliance on fossil fuels' position.
quote_text: We are looking only at new development.

name: Ariel Méndez
reasoning: When a homebuilder appealed Bend's newly adopted tree preservation code as a barrier to housing, Méndez publicly defended the code as a deliberate balance between housing needs and tree preservation rather than siding fully with either the developer or strict preservation advocates, and committed to a one-year evaluation. That posture -- applying a standard while remaining open to adjusting it -- fits 'consistent environmental standards while giving developers reasonable flexibility' more than a strict-preservation or fee-in-lieu-deregulation position.
quote_text: I've been to a lot of cities that don't have enough housing, but I've never been to a city where people say there are too many trees. City Council tried really hard to strike the right balance with this tree preservation code. We are still committed to evaluating it after one year to see how it's going.
